title: EV Charging Market Entry for a Utility
prompt: Your client is a regional electric utility considering entering the public EV (electric vehicle) fast-charging business in its home state. They would build and operate charging stations. Should they enter? Walk me through how you'd think about it.
background: The utility already generates and distributes electricity in the state.
The public fast-charging market in the state is currently served by two national players.
The client is comfortable with large, long-payback infrastructure investments.
Regulators are supportive of EV adoption.

clarifying_answers.What does success look like: A positive NPV business at scale within 7 years and strategic positioning for EV-driven electricity demand.
clarifying_answers.Any constraints: The client will not acquire an existing charging company; this is build-your-own.
clarifying_answers.What is the client's advantage: Low cost of capital, existing grid access, and brand trust with residents.

exhibits.name: State EV Market Sizing Inputs
exhibits.description: Inputs to size the public fast-charging opportunity.
exhibits.data: 4,000,000 cars registered in the state. EV penetration expected to reach 10% in 5 years = 400,000 EVs. ~20% of charging happens at public fast chargers. Average EV uses ~3,000 kWh/year; so public fast-charging demand ~ 400,000 x 3,000 x 20% = 240M kWh/year.

exhibits.name: Charger Unit Economics
exhibits.data: One stall costs $150,000 to build. It can deliver up to 150,000 kWh/year at target utilization. Gross margin to the operator is $0.20 per kWh after electricity cost. Operating cost per stall is $8,000/year.

good_framework: Market attractiveness: size and growth of public fast-charging demand in the state.
Competition: how the two incumbents are positioned; is there room for a third?
Client capabilities / right to win: grid access, cost of capital, brand, regulatory goodwill.
Economics: capex per stall, utilization, margin per kWh, payback / NPV.
Risks and decision: regulatory, technology, utilization ramp.

quant.question: What is the annual public fast-charging demand in the state in 5 years (kWh)?
quant.work: 400,000 EVs x 3,000 kWh/year x 20% public fast-charging = 240M kWh/year.

quant.question: How many stalls would be needed to serve that demand?
quant.work: 240M kWh / 150,000 kWh per stall = 1,600 stalls at target utilization.

quant.question: What is the annual gross profit per stall at target utilization?
quant.work: 150,000 kWh x $0.20 margin = $30,000 gross; minus $8,000 opex = ~$22,000/year. Payback on $150k capex ~7 years.

recommendation: Enter selectively. The market is sizable (~240M kWh/year, ~1,600 stalls) and the client has a real right to win (low capital cost, grid access, brand, regulatory support). Per-stall economics give ~$22k/year and a ~7-year payback — viable given the client's long-payback tolerance, but sensitive to utilization. Recommend a phased build in high-traffic corridors, validate utilization, then scale. Key risk: slower-than-expected EV adoption and incumbent price competition.
